newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels allege army offensive during talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels allege army offensive during talks.

text.p: The Marxist rebel group holding 72 hostages claimed on Sunday the army was "engaged in a major operation" to flush guerrillas out of their jungle strongholds while talks continue to end the hostage siege peacefully.

A senior Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader told Reuters the army was deploying more than 500 soldiers to sweep through the central jungle provinces of Oxapampa and Chanchamayo in a bid to destroy the group's military bases.

"The army has engaged in a major operation looking for our camps," Comrade Alejandro, who identified himself as a member of the MRTA's high-command, or policy-making body, said in a communication from the jungle county of Junin.

The army denies there is any military operation. But local media has reported several MRTA captures over the last two weeks in the central jungle -- the only area where the MRTA has a permanent armed presence.

Alejandro said the army had not captured any rebels in the operation, but had detained village peasants alleging they were members of the MRTA. "They want to find our camps but the only thing they are doing is detaining peasants," he said.

A leading Peruvian human rights group, APRODEH, issued a statement alleging that the whereabouts of four villagers in the area were still unknown after an army operation March 9 led to the detention of 21 peasants.
Comrade Alejandro claimed the army's action was in response to a series of Reuters reports late February about MRTA training and peasant collaboration in the central jungle.
Rebels in the area receive food, lodging and transport from jungle peasants, some of whom collaborate out of fear while others are MRTA sympathisers.

The army's jungle manoeuvres come at a time when neutral mediators are working energetically to find common ground between the two sides so that talks for a peaceful solution to the three-month-old hostage crisis in Lima can restart.

Members of an independent guarantors' commision, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, met rebel leader Nestor Cerpa at the besieged Japanese ambassador's home for about 90 minutes Saturday.
Cipriani entered the residence again Sunday alone to give Roman Catholic mass, local radio broadcasters said.
A police helicopter circled and hovered low over the residence twice on Sunday for about five minutes. There was no police explanation for the manoeuvre.

Saturday's meeting, the latest in a flurry of contacts with the rebels in the past week, added to signs that talks could advance again after being put on hold Wednesday to allow the two sides to "reflect" on their differences.

But the government has not ruled out using force. Local television showed a video Sunday of police SWAT teams practicing a violent takeover of a crude mock-up of the Japanese residence, complete with explosives and live bullets.
The MRTA's main demand is the release of some 400 jailed comrades -- a demand the government has refused to consider.
MRTA denied Sunday that it was responsible for a firebomb attack on a Lima textile factory, blaming it instead on government agents trying to embarrass the group.
"This type of action is never practiced by our movement," said MRTA in a statement sent to news media.

About eight armed men calling themselves MRTA rebels burst into the factory Saturday, tied up employees and set the place ablaze. Police later said they were unsure if the attackers were from MRTA or merely common criminals passing themselves off as rebels to throw police off their trail.

The rebels stormed a cocktail party at the ambassador's home Dec. 17 and took all the guests hostage. They released most of them but held on to the best bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and a long list of Japanese businessmen.
